Chapter 4: Difference Equations in Discrete-Time Macro Models

kapitaali.com
April 14, 2026

Business Cycle Dynamics

“In discrete time, every model is an iterated map. The question is whether that map has a fixed point, a cycle, or chaos.”

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 6 (time-series properties, HP filter); Ch. 10 (NKPC as a forward difference equation); Ch. 16 (rational expectations, forward solutions); Ch. 27 (RBC model log-linearized as a discrete system) [P:Ch.6, P:Ch.10, P:Ch.16, P:Ch.27]

4.1 Why Discrete Time? Data, Policy, and Computation¶

The choice between continuous and discrete time is not merely aesthetic. Several compelling reasons push modern macroeconomics toward discrete-time formulations.

Data observability. GDP is measured quarterly, inflation monthly, the federal funds rate daily. The natural time unit for policy analysis — the period between Federal Open Market Committee meetings — is six weeks. A continuous-time model that maps cleanly to quarterly data requires a discretization step anyway; it is simpler to start in discrete time.

Computational tractability. Value function iteration, the Kalman filter, the Metropolis–Hastings sampler for Bayesian DSGE estimation — all are inherently discrete. The state space must be discretized, time must be measured in steps, and probability distributions are approximated by finite grids.

Forward-looking equations. The New Keynesian Phillips Curve π^t=βEt[π^t+1]+κx^t\hat{\pi}_t = \beta\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \kappa\hat{x}_tπ^t​=βEt​[π^t+1​]+κx^t​ [P:Ch.10] and the Dynamic IS curve x^t=Et[x^t+1]−σ(it−Et[πt+1]−rtn)\hat{x}_t = \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] - \sigma(i_t - \mathbb{E}_t[\pi_{t+1}] - r^n_t)x^t​=Et​[x^t+1​]−σ(it​−Et​[πt+1​]−rtn​) are difference equations with expectations of future values. These arise naturally from discrete-time optimization but have no direct continuous-time analogue for policy analysis.

This chapter develops the theory of difference equations — the discrete-time counterpart to Chapter 3’s ODEs. Every result has a direct parallel in the continuous-time theory; the key substitution is eat↔λte^{at} \leftrightarrow \lambda^teat↔λt and the stability condition changes from a<0a < 0a<0 to ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1.

4.2 First-Order Linear Difference Equations¶

4.2.1 The Homogeneous Case¶

The equation xt+1=λxtx_{t+1} = \lambda x_txt+1​=λxt​ has the solution:

xt=λtx0.x_t = \lambda^t x_0.xt​=λtx0​.
(1)

Stability is determined by ∣λ∣|\lambda|∣λ∣:

  • ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1: xt→0x_t \to 0xt​→0 (stable).

  • ∣λ∣=1|\lambda| = 1∣λ∣=1: ∣xt∣=∣x0∣|x_t| = |x_0|∣xt​∣=∣x0​∣ constant (neutrally stable).

  • ∣λ∣>1|\lambda| > 1∣λ∣>1: ∣xt∣→∞|x_t| \to \infty∣xt​∣→∞ (unstable).

Theorem 4.1 (Stability of First-Order Difference Equations). The equilibrium x∗=0x^* = 0x∗=0 of xt+1=λxtx_{t+1} = \lambda x_txt+1​=λxt​ is globally asymptotically stable if and only if ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1.

4.2.2 The Nonhomogeneous Case¶

The equation xt+1=λxt+cx_{t+1} = \lambda x_t + cxt+1​=λxt​+c (with λ≠1\lambda \neq 1λ=1) has the general solution:

xt=λt(x0−x∗)+x∗,x∗=c1−λ.x_t = \lambda^t\left(x_0 - x^*\right) + x^*, \quad x^* = \frac{c}{1-\lambda}.xt​=λt(x0​−x∗)+x∗,x∗=1−λc​.
(2)

For ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1, xt→x∗x_t \to x^*xt​→x∗ as t→∞t \to \inftyt→∞.

Convergence speed: The gap xt−x∗x_t - x^*xt​−x∗ shrinks by factor λ\lambdaλ each period. After TTT periods, the gap is λT(x0−x∗)\lambda^T(x_0 - x^*)λT(x0​−x∗).

4.2.3 Backward vs. Forward Solutions¶

A crucial distinction in macroeconomics is between backward-looking (predeterminate) variables, whose current value is determined by past behavior, and forward-looking (free) variables, whose current value is determined by expected future behavior.

Backward solution for xt+1=λxt+cx_{t+1} = \lambda x_t + cxt+1​=λxt​+c: start from x0x_0x0​ and iterate forward. Requires ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1 for stability.

Forward solution for xt+1=λxt+cx_{t+1} = \lambda x_t + cxt+1​=λxt​+c: rearrange as xt=λ−1(xt+1−c)x_t = \lambda^{-1}(x_{t+1} - c)xt​=λ−1(xt+1​−c) and iterate forward:

xt=λ−Txt+T−cλ−1∑j=0T−1λ−j.x_t = \lambda^{-T}x_{t+T} - c\lambda^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{T-1}\lambda^{-j}.xt​=λ−Txt+T​−cλ−1j=0∑T−1​λ−j.
(3)

For the forward solution to be bounded (a transversality condition), we need ∣λ−Txt+T∣→0|\lambda^{-T}x_{t+T}| \to 0∣λ−Txt+T​∣→0 as T→∞T \to \inftyT→∞, which requires ∣λ∣>1|\lambda| > 1∣λ∣>1 (so ∣λ−T∣→0|\lambda^{-T}| \to 0∣λ−T∣→0). If ∣λ∣>1|\lambda| > 1∣λ∣>1, the forward solution is:

xt=−cλ−1+∑j=0∞λ−(j+1)Et[ct+j]=∑j=0∞λ−(j+1)Et[forcing variablet+j].x_t = -\frac{c}{\lambda - 1} + \sum_{j=0}^\infty \lambda^{-(j+1)}\mathbb{E}_t[c_{t+j}] = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \lambda^{-(j+1)}\mathbb{E}_t[\text{forcing variable}_{t+j}].xt​=−λ−1c​+j=0∑∞​λ−(j+1)Et​[ct+j​]=j=0∑∞​λ−(j+1)Et​[forcing variablet+j​].
(4)

This is the present-value formula structure that appears throughout the New Keynesian model. The NKPC forward solution π^t=κ∑j=0∞βjEt[x^t+j]\hat{\pi}_t = \kappa\sum_{j=0}^\infty \beta^j\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+j}]π^t​=κ∑j=0∞​βjEt​[x^t+j​] is exactly this form with λ=1/β>1\lambda = 1/\beta > 1λ=1/β>1 [P:Ch.10].

4.3 Second-Order Difference Equations¶

Second-order equations xt+2+pxt+1+qxt=cx_{t+2} + px_{t+1} + qx_t = cxt+2​+pxt+1​+qxt​=c appear in the multiplier–accelerator model of Samuelson (1939) [P:Ch.8] and in continuous-time models after discretization. The general solution is:

xt=C1λ1t+C2λ2t+x∗,x_t = C_1\lambda_1^t + C_2\lambda_2^t + x^*,xt​=C1​λ1t​+C2​λ2t​+x∗,
(5)

where λ1,λ2\lambda_1, \lambda_2λ1​,λ2​ are the roots of the characteristic equation:

λ2+pλ+q=0  ⟹  λ1,2=−p±p2−4q2,\lambda^2 + p\lambda + q = 0 \implies \lambda_{1,2} = \frac{-p \pm \sqrt{p^2 - 4q}}{2},λ2+pλ+q=0⟹λ1,2​=2−p±p2−4q​​,
(6)

and x∗=c/(1+p+q)x^* = c/(1 + p + q)x∗=c/(1+p+q) is the particular solution (assumed 1+p+q≠01 + p + q \neq 01+p+q=0). The constants C1C_1C1​, C2C_2C2​ are determined by two initial conditions x0x_0x0​ and x1x_1x1​.

Classification by roots:

Discriminant Δ=p2−4q\Delta = p^2 - 4qΔ=p2−4qRootsPath Type
Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0Two real roots λ1≠λ2\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2λ1​=λ2​Monotone (same sign) or S-shaped
Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0Repeated real root λ1=λ2=−p/2\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = -p/2λ1​=λ2​=−p/2Monotone or boundary case
Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0Complex conjugate pair λ=re±iθ\lambda = re^{\pm i\theta}λ=re±iθOscillatory

For complex roots λ=reiθ\lambda = re^{i\theta}λ=reiθ (where r=qr = \sqrt{q}r=q​ and θ=arctan⁡(4q−p2/(−p))\theta = \arctan(\sqrt{4q-p^2}/(-p))θ=arctan(4q−p2​/(−p))):

xt=x∗+rt(C1cos⁡(θt)+C2sin⁡(θt)).x_t = x^* + r^t(C_1\cos(\theta t) + C_2\sin(\theta t)).xt​=x∗+rt(C1​cos(θt)+C2​sin(θt)).
(7)

The system oscillates with period 2π/θ2\pi/\theta2π/θ and amplitude decaying like rtr^trt. Stability requires r=q<1r = \sqrt{q} < 1r=q​<1.

4.3.1 The Multiplier–Accelerator Model¶

Samuelson’s (1939) model of endogenous business cycles [P:Ch.8] sets:

Yt=Ct+It+G,Ct=bYt−1,It=v(Ct−Ct−1),Y_t = C_t + I_t + G, \quad C_t = bY_{t-1}, \quad I_t = v(C_t - C_{t-1}),Yt​=Ct​+It​+G,Ct​=bYt−1​,It​=v(Ct​−Ct−1​),
(8)

where bbb is the MPC and vvv is the accelerator. Substituting:

Yt=b(1+v)Yt−1−bvYt−2+G.Y_t = b(1+v)Y_{t-1} - bvY_{t-2} + G.Yt​=b(1+v)Yt−1​−bvYt−2​+G.
(9)

This is exactly a second-order difference equation with p=−b(1+v)p = -b(1+v)p=−b(1+v) and q=bvq = bvq=bv. The steady state is Y∗=G/(1−b)Y^* = G/(1-b)Y∗=G/(1−b).

Stability: Requires both roots ∣λ1,2∣<1|\lambda_{1,2}| < 1∣λ1,2​∣<1. Equivalently, the necessary and sufficient conditions are ∣p∣<1+q|p| < 1 + q∣p∣<1+q and q<1q < 1q<1, i.e., b(1+v)<1+bvb(1+v) < 1 + bvb(1+v)<1+bv (always true) and bv<1bv < 1bv<1. Stability requires bv<1bv < 1bv<1.

Business cycles arise from complex roots: When p2<4qp^2 < 4qp2<4q, i.e., b2(1+v)2<4bvb^2(1+v)^2 < 4bvb2(1+v)2<4bv, the roots are complex and the system oscillates. The amplitude r=bvr = \sqrt{bv}r=bv​ determines whether cycles decay (bv<1bv < 1bv<1), persist (bv=1bv = 1bv=1), or explode (bv>1bv > 1bv>1).

4.4 Systems of Linear Difference Equations¶

The discrete-time state-space form:

xt+1=Axt+But,\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = A\mathbf{x}_t + B\mathbf{u}_t,xt+1​=Axt​+But​,
(10)

where xt∈Rn\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^nxt​∈Rn is the state vector and ut∈Rm\mathbf{u}_t \in \mathbb{R}^mut​∈Rm is an exogenous input (shock or policy variable). This is the linearized DSGE model after log-linearization — the starting point of Parts VII.

General solution: Iterating the state equation:

xt=Atx0+∑j=0t−1AjBut−1−j.\mathbf{x}_t = A^t\mathbf{x}_0 + \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}A^j B\mathbf{u}_{t-1-j}.xt​=Atx0​+j=0∑t−1​AjBut−1−j​.
(11)

Using the eigendecomposition A=PDP−1A = PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1:

xt=PDtP−1x0+∑j=0t−1PDjP−1But−1−j.\mathbf{x}_t = PD^tP^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0 + \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}PD^jP^{-1}B\mathbf{u}_{t-1-j}.xt​=PDtP−1x0​+j=0∑t−1​PDjP−1But−1−j​.
(12)

Stability: Requires all eigenvalues of AAA to satisfy ∣λi∣<1|\lambda_i| < 1∣λi​∣<1.

Impulse response: The response of x\mathbf{x}x to a unit shock u0=ej\mathbf{u}_0 = \mathbf{e}_ju0​=ej​ (with ut=0\mathbf{u}_t = \mathbf{0}ut​=0 for t>0t > 0t>0) at horizon hhh is Ah−1BejA^{h-1}B\mathbf{e}_jAh−1Bej​ — the jjj-th column of Ah−1BA^{h-1}BAh−1B. This is computed efficiently as AhvA^h\mathbf{v}Ahv using repeated matrix multiplication or via the eigendecomposition.

4.5 Forward-Looking Difference Equations and the Minimum State Variable Solution¶

The distinctive challenge of modern macroeconomics is that many key equations involve expected future values of endogenous variables. The NKPC is π^t=βEt[π^t+1]+κx^t\hat{\pi}_t = \beta\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \kappa\hat{x}_tπ^t​=βEt​[π^t+1​]+κx^t​; the DIS is x^t=Et[x^t+1]−σ(i^t−Et[π^t+1]−r^tn)\hat{x}_t = \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] - \sigma(\hat{i}_t - \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] - \hat{r}^n_t)x^t​=Et​[x^t+1​]−σ(i^t​−Et​[π^t+1​]−r^tn​). These are expectational difference equations with no unique solution without additional restrictions.

Definition 4.1 (Minimum State Variable Solution). The minimum state variable (MSV) solution is the unique solution of a linear expectational difference equation that expresses each endogenous variable as a linear function of the minimal set of state variables — typically the exogenous forcing variables and any predetermined (backward-looking) variables.

McCallum’s (1983) algorithm for finding the MSV solution:

Algorithm 4.1 (McCallum’s Undetermined Coefficients).

Given the expectational system yt=AEt[yt+1]+Czt\mathbf{y}_t = A\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + C\mathbf{z}_tyt​=AEt​[yt+1​]+Czt​ where zt\mathbf{z}_tzt​ is a vector of exogenous state variables with law of motion zt+1=Φzt+εt+1\mathbf{z}_{t+1} = \Phi\mathbf{z}_t + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t+1}zt+1​=Φzt​+εt+1​:

  1. Guess an MSV solution: yt=Ωzt\mathbf{y}_t = \Omega\mathbf{z}_tyt​=Ωzt​ (endogenous variables are linear functions of exogenous states).

  2. Compute Et[yt+1]=ΩEt[zt+1]=ΩΦzt\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] = \Omega\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{z}_{t+1}] = \Omega\Phi\mathbf{z}_tEt​[yt+1​]=ΩEt​[zt+1​]=ΩΦzt​.

  3. Substitute into the original equation: Ωzt=AΩΦzt+Czt\Omega\mathbf{z}_t = A\Omega\Phi\mathbf{z}_t + C\mathbf{z}_tΩzt​=AΩΦzt​+Czt​.

  4. Match coefficients: Ω=AΩΦ+C\Omega = A\Omega\Phi + CΩ=AΩΦ+C.

  5. Solve this matrix equation for Ω\OmegaΩ. This is a discrete Sylvester equation of the form Ω−AΩΦ=C\Omega - A\Omega\Phi = CΩ−AΩΦ=C.

The Sylvester equation Ω−AΩΦ=C\Omega - A\Omega\Phi = CΩ−AΩΦ=C can be vectorized: vec(Ω)(I−Φ′⊗A)=vec(C)\text{vec}(\Omega)(I - \Phi' \otimes A) = \text{vec}(C)vec(Ω)(I−Φ′⊗A)=vec(C), which is a linear system in vec(Ω)\text{vec}(\Omega)vec(Ω). It has a unique solution when (I−Φ′⊗A)(I - \Phi' \otimes A)(I−Φ′⊗A) is nonsingular — equivalently, when no eigenvalue of Φ\PhiΦ equals the reciprocal of any eigenvalue of AAA.

4.5.1 Application: The NK Model Under a Taylor Rule¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 10, Ch. 23 [P:Ch.10, P:Ch.23]

The three-equation NK model:

x^t=Et[x^t+1]−σ(i^t−Et[π^t+1]−r^tn)\hat{x}_t = \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] - \sigma(\hat{i}_t - \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] - \hat{r}^n_t)x^t​=Et​[x^t+1​]−σ(i^t​−Et​[π^t+1​]−r^tn​)
(13)

π^t=βEt[π^t+1]+κx^t\hat{\pi}_t = \beta\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \kappa\hat{x}_tπ^t​=βEt​[π^t+1​]+κx^t​
(14)

i^t=ϕππ^t+ϕyx^t+r^tn\hat{i}_t = \phi_\pi\hat{\pi}_t + \phi_y\hat{x}_t + \hat{r}^n_ti^t​=ϕπ​π^t​+ϕy​x^t​+r^tn​
(15)

Substituting the Taylor rule into the DIS:

x^t=Et[x^t+1]−σϕππ^t−σϕyx^t+σr^tn−σEt[π^t+1]+σr^tn.\hat{x}_t = \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] - \sigma\phi_\pi\hat{\pi}_t - \sigma\phi_y\hat{x}_t + \sigma\hat{r}^n_t - \sigma\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \sigma\hat{r}^n_t.x^t​=Et​[x^t+1​]−σϕπ​π^t​−σϕy​x^t​+σr^tn​−σEt​[π^t+1​]+σr^tn​.
(16)

Wait — let us use the compact matrix form. Stack yt=(π^t,x^t)′\mathbf{y}_t = (\hat{\pi}_t, \hat{x}_t)'yt​=(π^t​,x^t​)′ and note that both are jump variables (free to adjust at each date). The system can be written:

(10σϕπ1+σϕy)⏟≡Γ0yt=(βκσ1)⏟≡Γ1Et[yt+1]+(0σ)⏟≡Ψr^tn.\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \sigma\phi_\pi & 1+\sigma\phi_y \end{pmatrix}}_{\equiv\Gamma_0} \mathbf{y}_t = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \beta & \kappa \\ \sigma & 1 \end{pmatrix}}_{\equiv\Gamma_1} \mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \sigma \end{pmatrix}}_{\equiv\Psi}\hat{r}^n_t.≡Γ0​(1σϕπ​​01+σϕy​​)​​yt​=≡Γ1​(βσ​κ1​)​​Et​[yt+1​]+≡Ψ(0σ​)​​r^tn​.
(17)

This is the canonical form Γ0yt=Γ1Et[yt+1]+Ψzt\Gamma_0\mathbf{y}_t = \Gamma_1\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + \Psi z_tΓ0​yt​=Γ1​Et​[yt+1​]+Ψzt​, which we solve via yt=Γ0−1Γ1Et[yt+1]+Γ0−1Ψzt\mathbf{y}_t = \Gamma_0^{-1}\Gamma_1\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + \Gamma_0^{-1}\Psi z_tyt​=Γ0−1​Γ1​Et​[yt+1​]+Γ0−1​Ψzt​. Let A=Γ0−1Γ1A = \Gamma_0^{-1}\Gamma_1A=Γ0−1​Γ1​ and C=Γ0−1ΨC = \Gamma_0^{-1}\PsiC=Γ0−1​Ψ. The MSV solution is yt=Ωzt\mathbf{y}_t = \Omega z_tyt​=Ωzt​ where Ω\OmegaΩ solves the scalar Sylvester equation Ω−AΩρr=C\Omega - A\Omega\rho_r = CΩ−AΩρr​=C (since zt=r^tnz_t = \hat{r}^n_tzt​=r^tn​ follows AR(1) with ϕ=ρr\phi = \rho_rϕ=ρr​).

Determinacy: The system has a unique bounded solution (MSV solution is the only equilibrium) iff the number of eigenvalues of A=Γ0−1Γ1A = \Gamma_0^{-1}\Gamma_1A=Γ0−1​Γ1​ outside the unit circle equals the number of free variables — here, both π^t\hat{\pi}_tπ^t​ and x^t\hat{x}_tx^t​ are free, so we need exactly 2 eigenvalues of AAA outside the unit circle. This is the Blanchard–Kahn condition for this model (developed fully in Chapter 28).

The Taylor principle ϕπ>1\phi_\pi > 1ϕπ​>1 ensures this: in the 2×2 NK model, ϕπ>1\phi_\pi > 1ϕπ​>1 implies both eigenvalues of AAA have modulus greater than 1, satisfying the Blanchard–Kahn condition. This is the formal derivation of the result stated in Principles Ch. 23 [P:Ch.23.1] that the Taylor principle is necessary and sufficient for determinacy.

4.6 Stability Analysis and the Unit Circle¶

For a system xt+1=Axt\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = A\mathbf{x}_txt+1​=Axt​, stability is determined by the eigenvalues of AAA relative to the unit circle in the complex plane.

Definition 4.2 (Stable, Unstable, and Centre Subspaces). Decompose Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn into three subspaces based on eigenvalues:

  • Stable subspace EsE^sEs: spanned by generalised eigenvectors corresponding to ∣λi∣<1|\lambda_i| < 1∣λi​∣<1.

  • Unstable subspace EuE^uEu: spanned by generalised eigenvectors corresponding to ∣λi∣>1|\lambda_i| > 1∣λi​∣>1.

  • Centre subspace EcE^cEc: spanned by generalised eigenvectors corresponding to ∣λi∣=1|\lambda_i| = 1∣λi​∣=1.

For the DSGE model with nsn_sns​ predetermined variables and nfn_fnf​ free (jump) variables, the Blanchard–Kahn condition requires:

Number of eigenvalues of AAA outside unit circle = number of free variables nfn_fnf​.

When this holds, the model has a unique bounded rational expectations equilibrium. When there are too few eigenvalues outside the unit circle, there are multiple equilibria (indeterminacy — sunspot equilibria exist). When there are too many, no bounded equilibrium exists (the model “explodes”).

Checking stability in APL:

⎕IO←0 ⋄ ⎕ML←1

A ← 2 2 ⍴ 1.2 0.3 ¯0.1 0.85

⍝ 1. Calculate Trace and Determinant
tr ← A[0;0] + A[1;1]
det ← (A[0;0]×A[1;1]) - (A[0;1]×A[1;0])

⍝ 2. Solve Quadratic: λ² - tr*λ + det = 0
⍝ We calculate the two roots separately to avoid vector confusion
disc ← (tr*2) - 4×det
root_part ← disc * 0.5

eig1 ← (tr + root_part) ÷ 2
eig2 ← (tr - root_part) ÷ 2
eig_vals ← eig1, eig2

⍝ 3. Moduli and BK Condition
moduli ← | eig_vals
n_outside ← +/ moduli > 1

⍝ Display
'Eigenvalues:' eig_vals
'Moduli:     ' moduli
'BK Count:   ' n_outside

4.7 Worked Example: Solving the Two-Equation NK System¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 10, Ch. 23 [P:Ch.Ch.10, P:Ch.23]

Consider the simplified NK model with only a cost-push shock utu_tut​:

π^t=βEt[π^t+1]+κx^t+ut,ut=ρuut−1+εt\hat{\pi}_t = \beta\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \kappa\hat{x}_t + u_t, \quad u_t = \rho_u u_{t-1} + \varepsilon_tπ^t​=βEt​[π^t+1​]+κx^t​+ut​,ut​=ρu​ut−1​+εt​
(18)

x^t=Et[x^t+1]−σϕππ^t−σϕyx^t.\hat{x}_t = \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] - \sigma\phi_\pi\hat{\pi}_t - \sigma\phi_y\hat{x}_t.x^t​=Et​[x^t+1​]−σϕπ​π^t​−σϕy​x^t​.
(19)

Calibration: β=0.99\beta = 0.99β=0.99, κ=0.15\kappa = 0.15κ=0.15, σ=1\sigma = 1σ=1, ϕπ=1.5\phi_\pi = 1.5ϕπ​=1.5, ϕy=0.5\phi_y = 0.5ϕy​=0.5, ρu=0.7\rho_u = 0.7ρu​=0.7.

Step 1: Canonical form. Stack yt=(π^t,x^t,ut)′\mathbf{y}_t = (\hat{\pi}_t, \hat{x}_t, u_t)'yt​=(π^t​,x^t​,ut​)′ (the shock is a state variable since it is predetermined). Write:

Γ0yt=Γ1Et[yt+1]+noise,\Gamma_0\mathbf{y}_t = \Gamma_1\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + \text{noise},Γ0​yt​=Γ1​Et​[yt+1​]+noise,
(20)

but since utu_tut​ is predetermined, it belongs in the state vector rather than as a free variable.

Step 2: MSV guess. Since the only state is utu_tut​, guess:

π^t=ωπut,x^t=ωxut.\hat{\pi}_t = \omega_\pi u_t, \quad \hat{x}_t = \omega_x u_t.π^t​=ωπ​ut​,x^t​=ωx​ut​.
(21)

Step 3: Solve for coefficients. Substituting π^t=ωπut\hat{\pi}_t = \omega_\pi u_tπ^t​=ωπ​ut​, x^t=ωxut\hat{x}_t = \omega_x u_tx^t​=ωx​ut​, and Et[π^t+1]=ωπρuut\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] = \omega_\pi\rho_u u_tEt​[π^t+1​]=ωπ​ρu​ut​, Et[x^t+1]=ωxρuut\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] = \omega_x\rho_u u_tEt​[x^t+1​]=ωx​ρu​ut​ into the NKPC:

ωπut=βωπρuut+κωxut+ut  ⟹  ωπ(1−βρu)=κωx+1.\omega_\pi u_t = \beta\omega_\pi\rho_u u_t + \kappa\omega_x u_t + u_t \implies \omega_\pi(1 - \beta\rho_u) = \kappa\omega_x + 1.ωπ​ut​=βωπ​ρu​ut​+κωx​ut​+ut​⟹ωπ​(1−βρu​)=κωx​+1.
(22)

And into the DIS (with Taylor rule substituted):

ωxut=ωxρuut−σϕπωπut−σϕyωxut  ⟹  ωx(1−ρu+σϕy)=−σϕπωπ.\omega_x u_t = \omega_x\rho_u u_t - \sigma\phi_\pi\omega_\pi u_t - \sigma\phi_y\omega_x u_t \implies \omega_x(1 - \rho_u + \sigma\phi_y) = -\sigma\phi_\pi\omega_\pi.ωx​ut​=ωx​ρu​ut​−σϕπ​ωπ​ut​−σϕy​ωx​ut​⟹ωx​(1−ρu​+σϕy​)=−σϕπ​ωπ​.
(23)

Step 4: Solve the 2×2 system. Let a=1−βρua = 1 - \beta\rho_ua=1−βρu​, b=1−ρu+σϕyb = 1 - \rho_u + \sigma\phi_yb=1−ρu​+σϕy​, c=σϕπc = \sigma\phi_\pic=σϕπ​:

ωπ=κωx+1a,ωx=−cωπb.\omega_\pi = \frac{\kappa\omega_x + 1}{a}, \quad \omega_x = \frac{-c\omega_\pi}{b}.ωπ​=aκωx​+1​,ωx​=b−cωπ​​.
(24)

Substituting the second into the first:

ωπ=−cκωπ/b+1a  ⟹  ωπ(a+cκb)=1  ⟹  ωπ=bab+cκ.\omega_\pi = \frac{-c\kappa\omega_\pi/b + 1}{a} \implies \omega_\pi\left(a + \frac{c\kappa}{b}\right) = 1 \implies \omega_\pi = \frac{b}{ab + c\kappa}.ωπ​=a−cκωπ​/b+1​⟹ωπ​(a+bcκ​)=1⟹ωπ​=ab+cκb​.
(25)

Then ωx=−cωπ/b=−c/(ab+cκ)\omega_x = -c\omega_\pi/b = -c/(ab + c\kappa)ωx​=−cωπ​/b=−c/(ab+cκ).

Step 5: Numerical evaluation.

a=1−0.99×0.7=0.307a = 1 - 0.99 \times 0.7 = 0.307a=1−0.99×0.7=0.307

b=1−0.7+1×0.5=0.8b = 1 - 0.7 + 1 \times 0.5 = 0.8b=1−0.7+1×0.5=0.8

c=1×1.5=1.5c = 1 \times 1.5 = 1.5c=1×1.5=1.5

ab+cκ=0.307×0.8+1.5×0.15=0.2456+0.225=0.4706ab + c\kappa = 0.307 \times 0.8 + 1.5 \times 0.15 = 0.2456 + 0.225 = 0.4706ab+cκ=0.307×0.8+1.5×0.15=0.2456+0.225=0.4706

ωπ=0.8/0.4706=1.700\omega_\pi = 0.8/0.4706 = 1.700ωπ​=0.8/0.4706=1.700

ωx=−1.5/0.4706=−3.188\omega_x = -1.5/0.4706 = -3.188ωx​=−1.5/0.4706=−3.188

Interpretation: A positive cost-push shock of 1 unit raises inflation by 1.700 and lowers the output gap by 3.188. The large output gap response reflects the central bank’s aggressive tightening (high ϕπ=1.5\phi_\pi = 1.5ϕπ​=1.5) in response to the inflation increase.

4.8 The Cobweb Model and Expectational Stability¶

The classic cobweb model illustrates how adaptive versus rational expectations change the dynamics of a market with production lags.

Supply: Qts=a+bPteQ_t^s = a + b P_t^eQts​=a+bPte​ (firms produce based on expected price) Demand: Qtd=c−dPtQ_t^d = c - d P_tQtd​=c−dPt​ (consumers respond to actual price)

Market clearing: Qts=QtdQ_t^s = Q_t^dQts​=Qtd​, so:

Pt=c−ad−bdPte.P_t = \frac{c - a}{d} - \frac{b}{d}P_t^e.Pt​=dc−a​−db​Pte​.
(26)

Under adaptive expectations Pte=Pt−1P_t^e = P_{t-1}Pte​=Pt−1​ (naive: expect last period’s price):

Pt=c−ad−bdPt−1.P_t = \frac{c-a}{d} - \frac{b}{d}P_{t-1}.Pt​=dc−a​−db​Pt−1​.
(27)

This is a first-order difference equation with coefficient −b/d-b/d−b/d. Stability requires ∣−b/d∣<1|{-b/d}| < 1∣−b/d∣<1, i.e., supply is more elastic than demand (b<db < db<d). If supply is more elastic (b>db > db>d), the cobweb explodes.

Under rational expectations Pte=E[Pt]P_t^e = \mathbb{E}[P_t]Pte​=E[Pt​] (firms correctly anticipate the equilibrium price), the market always clears at the rational expectations equilibrium price P∗=(c−a)/(b+d)P^* = (c-a)/(b+d)P∗=(c−a)/(b+d) — no cobweb dynamics at all. Rational expectations “flatten” the cobweb by eliminating the lag between expectation and realization.

This example, while simple, illustrates the fundamental point of Principles Chapter 16 [P:Ch.16]: rational expectations can eliminate systematic forecast errors and with them the price dynamics that drive business cycles. Whether prices and wages are actually set as rationally as this model implies is an empirical question — but it sets the theoretical benchmark.

Exercise 4.2 (Python — Stability Diagram)¶

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

b_vals = np.linspace(0, 1, 100)
v_vals = np.linspace(0, 3, 100)
B, V = np.meshgrid(b_vals, v_vals)

# Characteristic roots
p = -B*(1+V)
q = B*V
disc = p**2 - 4*q
lambda_modulus = np.where(disc >= 0,
    np.maximum(np.abs((-p + np.sqrt(np.abs(disc)))/2),
               np.abs((-p - np.sqrt(np.abs(disc)))/2)),
    np.sqrt(q))  # for complex roots, modulus = sqrt(q)

stable = lambda_modulus < 1
oscillatory = (disc < 0) & stable

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.contourf(B, V, stable.astype(int), levels=[0.5,1.5], colors=['lightblue'], alpha=0.5)
ax.contour(B, V, oscillatory.astype(int), levels=[0.5], colors=['red'])
ax.set_xlabel('MPC (b)'); ax.set_ylabel('Accelerator (v)')
ax.set_title('Stability diagram: blue=stable, red boundary=oscillatory')
plt.show()

Exercise 4.3 (Julia — MSV Solution)¶

# MSV solution for arbitrary NK calibration
function msv_nk(; beta=0.99, kappa=0.15, sigma=1.0,
                  phi_pi=1.5, phi_y=0.5, rho_u=0.7)
    a = 1 - beta*rho_u
    b = 1 - rho_u + sigma*phi_y
    c = sigma*phi_pi
    denom = a*b + c*kappa
    omega_pi = b / denom
    omega_x  = -c / denom
    return (omega_pi=omega_pi, omega_x=omega_x)
end

sol = msv_nk()
println("ω_π = $(round(sol.omega_pi, digits=3))")
println("ω_x = $(round(sol.omega_x, digits=3))")

# Sweep over phi_pi to show determinacy
phi_pis = 0.5:0.1:3.0
for φ in phi_pis
    s = msv_nk(phi_pi=φ)
    println("φ_π = $φ: ω_π = $(round(s.omega_pi,digits=3)), ω_x = $(round(s.omega_x,digits=3))")
end

Exercise 4.4 (R — Forward Solution)¶

# Forward solution of NKPC: pi_t = kappa * sum_{j>=0} beta^j E_t[x_{t+j}]
# Given AR(1) output gap: x_t = rho_x * x_{t-1} + eps_t
kappa <- 0.15; beta <- 0.99; rho_x <- 0.8

# Closed-form: pi_t = kappa/(1-beta*rho_x) * x_t
omega_pi_forward <- kappa / (1 - beta*rho_x)
cat("π_t = ", round(omega_pi_forward, 4), "* x_t\n")

# Simulate and verify numerically
T <- 1000
set.seed(42)
x <- filter(rnorm(T, sd=0.1), rho_x, method="recursive")
pi_formula <- omega_pi_forward * x

# Compare to direct present-value calculation
pi_pv <- sapply(1:(T-50), function(t) {
  kappa * sum(sapply(0:49, function(j) beta^j * x[t+j]))
})
cat("Max discrepancy:", max(abs(pi_formula[1:(T-50)] - pi_pv)), "\n")

4.10 Chapter Summary¶

Key results:

  • First-order linear difference equations xt+1=λxt+cx_{t+1} = \lambda x_t + cxt+1​=λxt​+c are stable iff ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1, with convergence rate ∣λ∣|\lambda|∣λ∣ and steady state x∗=c/(1−λ)x^* = c/(1-\lambda)x∗=c/(1−λ).

  • Backward solutions require ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1 (predetermined variables); forward solutions require ∣λ∣>1|\lambda| > 1∣λ∣>1 (free/jump variables). The present-value formula structure of the NKPC arises from the forward solution with ∣λ∣=1/β>1|\lambda| = 1/\beta > 1∣λ∣=1/β>1.

  • Second-order equations xt+2+pxt+1+qxt=cx_{t+2} + px_{t+1} + qx_t = cxt+2​+pxt+1​+qxt​=c generate oscillatory dynamics when the discriminant p2−4q<0p^2 - 4q < 0p2−4q<0; stability requires q<1\sqrt{q} < 1q​<1.

  • The MSV solution of an expectational difference equation is found by guessing a linear function of state variables and matching coefficients — the Sylvester equation.

  • The Blanchard–Kahn condition for a unique bounded rational expectations equilibrium: number of eigenvalues outside the unit circle equals number of free variables.

  • In APL: matrix powers A⍣h compute impulse responses efficiently; the scan \ collects path histories; rho_u * ⍳T generates geometric decay sequences directly.

Connections forward: Chapter 14 revisits difference equations in the multiplier–accelerator context. Chapter 18 develops the full rational expectations solution methodology (undetermined coefficients, the Sims algorithm). Chapter 28 provides the definitive treatment of the Blanchard–Kahn conditions and the QZ decomposition algorithm for DSGE models.
